analysis.one_liner: Closes the loophole exempting oil and gas drilling waste from hazardous waste rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 73 Democratic cosponsors, never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1988, waste from drilling for oil and gas — drilling fluids, produced water, and other byproducts — has been exempt from the nation's hazardous waste rules, even though it can contain toxic chemicals. This bill directed the EPA to test that waste against hazardous waste criteria, regulate whatever qualifies as hazardous, and require groundwater monitoring, location standards, and cleanup and financial-assurance rules for landfills that take the rest. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near oil and gas wells, drilling waste pits, or the landfills and injection sites that take drilling waste, because their air, groundwater, and drinking water would face new federal protection. Communities near landfills get monitoring and cleanup requirements; taxpayers benefit from financial assurance rules that shift cleanup costs back to waste handlers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near drilling waste sites

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to determine whether drilling fluids, produced waters, and other oil, gas, and geothermal waste meet hazardous waste criteria, and to list and regulate any that do, with rules for generators, transporters, and disposal facilities.

Requires new landfill criteria for non-hazardous drilling waste, including groundwater monitoring to detect contamination, acceptable location standards, and corrective action and financial assurance.

Lets the EPA tailor requirements to the special characteristics of drilling waste as long as they still protect human health and the environment, acknowledging cost and feasibility concerns in the bill itself.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, geothermal operators, and the waste disposal companies handling their byproducts, who would face testing, handling, tracking, and disposal costs — some of which could be passed to consumers through energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers and waste handlers

drawbacks.text: Regulating drilling waste as hazardous would raise disposal costs for oil and gas producers, which could fall on consumers through higher energy prices and reduce drilling activity, especially for smaller operators.
The bill gave the EPA only one year to complete a full hazardous waste determination and write disposal regulations, a compressed timeline that could have produced rushed or legally fragile rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: closing the exemption protects groundwater and communities near waste sites, but raises disposal costs in a margin-sensitive industry. The bill already softened the cost by allowing modified standards tailored to drilling waste, so the main risk is implementation, not design.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee — which referred it to a subcommittee the day after introduction — and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 6, 2017, with 37 original cosponsors, and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, which is where the record ends; no further action was taken for the rest of the 115th Congress.
It accumulated 73 cosponsors, all Democrats, but the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the full committee or on the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and waste handlers keep the 1988 exemption from hazardous waste rules, avoiding new testing, handling, and disposal costs; nearby communities continue to bear the contamination risk without federal monitoring requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers keep the waste exemption

for.name: Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end the oil and gas waste exemption and referred it to Energy and Commerce.

for.name: 73 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats, building a large but insufficient bloc of support to move it in committee.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; controlled whether the bill got a hearing or vote
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, letting it die in committee for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 73 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support on record, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their decades-old exemption from hazardous waste rules, forcing testing and regulated disposal of drilling fluids and produced water. Industry's interest in keeping the exemption runs against residents whose groundwater and communities absorb the waste.
The bill covered geothermal production waste in the same exemption-closing scheme, subjecting it to hazardous waste testing and regulation.

industries.industry: Hazardous and industrial waste disposal companies
industries.note: New hazardous waste designations and stricter landfill criteria would have created regulated demand for compliant treatment, storage, and disposal services, alongside groundwater monitoring and financial assurance requirements that lift standards for communities.
